Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) transforms this process into a closed-loop, experimentally grounded discovery ecosystem. This Review provides a roadmap for this paradigm, demonstrating how AI, high-throughput testing, and nanoscale design converge to generate clinically translatable nanotherapeutics. We emphasize the necessity of standardized multimodal data-spanning pharmacokinetic, biodistribution, and drug-release profiles-anchored strictly to validated biological phenomena. Furthermore, we evaluate an algorithmic spectrum, ranging from classical machine learning to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and reinforcement learning (RL), to align models with specific formulation objectives. To bridge computational design and empirical reality, we examine how high-throughput technologies, such as robotic laboratories and in vivo DNA-barcoding multiplexing, operationalize the \\\"Design-Make-Test-Analyze\\\" (DMTA) cycle for dynamic model recalibration. Ultimately, this review demonstrates how integrating AI, physical constraints, and automated validation accelerates the rational design of next-generation nanomedicines.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.78125\", \"pmid\": \"42934944\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13710834\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.78125\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13710834\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13710834?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"The rise of agentic AI in drug discover…

Machine Learning (2026) 115:109
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10994-025-06955-2
Abstract
The paper surveys automated scientific discovery, from equation discovery and symbolic 
regression to autonomous discovery systems and agents. It discusses the individual ap -
proaches from a "big picture" perspective and in context, but also discusses open issues 
and recent topics like the various roles of deep neural networks in this area, aiding in the 
discovery of human-interpretable knowledge. Further, we will present closed-loop sci -
entific discovery systems, starting with the pioneering work on the Adam system up to 
current efforts in fields from material science to astronomy. Finally, we will elaborate on 
autonomy from a machine learning perspective, but also in analogy to the autonomy lev -
els in autonomous driving. The maximal level, level five, is defined to require no human 
intervention at all in the production of scientific knowledge. Achieving this is one step 
towards solving the Nobel Turing Grand Challenge to develop AI Scientists: AI systems 
capable of making Nobel-quality scientific discoveries highly autonomously at a level 
comparable, and possibly superior, to the best human scientists by 2050.

labs · AI scientist · Nobel Turing challenge

Reinforcement Learning (RL) provides a dynamic framework for asset allocation, but manually specifying reward functions that generalize across diverse market regimes remains a significant challenge. Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) offers a principled alternative by recovering reward signals from expert behavior. However, when demonstrations originate from multiple experts with divergent investment objectives, the collective expert distribution becomes inherently multi-modal. Multiple distinct actions may be simultaneously rational for a given market state, and conventional IRL frameworks are not designed to accommodate this complexity. We propose Multi-Expert Inverse Reinforcement Learning (ME-IRL), a framework that employs an Energy-Based Model (EBM) as a reward network to model this multi-modal collective expert distribution. Rather than specifying objectives a priori or aggregating expert behaviors at the action-level, ME-IRL performs reward-level inference that encodes interactions among conflicting financial objectives. This is achieved through a Transformer-based architecture utilizing cross-attention between state and action representations to explicitly model cross-sectional asset dependencies.
